meta_jurisdiction_context.legal_system_doctrine: Hybrid - Canada is a federal common-law jurisdiction, while Quebec is a bi-juridical 'mixed' legal system in which private-law matters, including corporate, commercial and property matters within provincial competence, are governed by the civil law tradition of the Code civil du Quebec; public law, constitutional law and federal corporate law follow the common law tradition.

Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), in force for Canada 30 December 2018

Canada-United Kingdom Trade Continuity Agreement, in force 1 April 2021

Canada's network of more than 90 bilateral double-tax-avoidance agreements (DTAAs) under the OECD Model, including the Canada-US Convention (1980, as amended) and the Canada-China DTA (1986, as amended by the 2013 Protocol)

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Original letter stamped and signed by the bank, signature notarized; apostille or consular legalization required if the bank is located outside Canada; document must be dated within 90 days

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Consent to act as director (Consentement du candidat administrateur) under the Quebec Business Corporations Act, CQLR c. S-31.1, art. 107

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: All directors, officers, shareholders and UBOs must be screened, before incorporation, against (i) the consolidated United Nations Security Council sanctions lists; (ii) Canadian sanctions under the Special Economic Measures Act, the United Nations Act and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act (Magnitsky list); (iii) the FINTRAD-listed terrorist entities and the Criminal Code regulatory listing; (iv) the OFAC SDN and sectoral sanctions lists, mandatory where any USD-denominated wire transfer, US correspondent banking or US counterparty is involved; and (v) multilateral development-bank debarment lists, in particular the World Bank and Asian Development Bank, given the civil-infrastructure CAD/BIM subcontracting profile. Any positive match, or the presence of a domestic or foreign Politically Exposed Person (FINTRAC definition), triggers mandatory enhanced due diligence (source-of-wealth documents, senior legal sign-off and UBO re-verification), irrespective of the entity's otherwise low-risk AML tier.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Registraire des entreprises du Quebec (REQ) u2013 online services portal at www.registreentreprises.gouv.qc.ca; parallel federal NUANS clearance through Corporations Canada at www.ic.gc.ca/CR
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Under the Charter of the French Language, CQLR c. C-11, the corporate name and all mandatory legal publicity of a Quebec business must be in French. An English-only name is accepted only where (i) it is a recognized trademark within the meaning of the Charter, (ii) the name is composed of a proper noun or distinctive coinage having no French equivalent, or (iii) a parallel French version is registered as the legal name. The legal name must bear a Quebec-approved legal element (Inc., Ltee, Corp., Corporation, Limitee, Incorporee). Non-Latin scripts must be transliterated into Latin characters, and the French version governs all statutory filings and invoicing.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Ingenieur / Engineer / Genie - protected professional title under the Professional Code, CQLR c. C-26, art. 32; requires a permit of the Ordre des ingenieurs du Quebec (OIQ)
Universite / University / Ecole polytechnique (in a manner implying public accreditation)
Canada (requires approval of the Governor in Council for federal names)
Quebec / Gouvernement / Municipal (false suggestion of public authority)
Architecte / Arpenteur-geometre / Ingenieur (other reserved professional titles under the Professional Code)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: The REQ name reservation is valid for 90 days and may be renewed once for a further 90 days. Upon a refusal or a conditional-name decision, the applicant may, within 30 days of receiving notice, (i) file an informal reconsideration request via the REQ online 'Demande de revision' service, and (ii) if the refusal is maintained, institute a formal appeal before the Administrative Division of the Court of Quebec within 30 days under arts. 22-23 of the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises, CQLR c. P-44.1. At the federal level, a NUANS/name rejection may be contested by written representation to the Director under s. 20 of the Canada Business Corporations Act and thereafter by judicial review to the Federal Court of Canada within 30 days. During appeal, the applicant may simultaneously reserve a secondary or alternative French name to avoid delay.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Conditionally permitted. Quebec law requires a genuine physical registered office (siege social) within the province, capable of receiving service of process and preserving corporate records; a mere post-office box is invalid. Commercial 'virtual office' providers that supply a permanent Quebec street address, reception staffing, mail forwarding and hours of attendance are accepted by the REQ and by Canadian banks for low-risk, non-regulated professional-services companies, provided the address is not a shared shell and the corporate records are physically accessible at that location. The REQ requires disclosure of the exact municipality, civic address and the nature of the premises; the registered office must appear in the enterprise register and in articles of incorporation.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low (quantified risk of approximately 5% per operating year for a non-regulated, low-risk professional-services company with an ordinary commercial virtual address in Montreal or Quebec City). The likelihood rises to approximately 15% if the corporate name includes a regulated professional title (e.g., engineering), if the virtual office is a third-party co-working hall shared by multiple registrants, or if Revenu Quebec or FINTRAC initiates a compliance verification following the opening of multi-currency bank accounts or high-volume cross-border wire activity.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (Québec), CQLR c S-31.1 — ss. 9-17 (Articles of Incorporation and certificate of incorporation), s. 13 (commencement of existence), ss. 34-52 (authorized share capital and subscription), ss. 111-121 (board of directors, management and by-laws), ss. 140-145 (registered office and corporate records); public registration and legal publicity governed by the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises, CQLR c P-44.1, ss. 22-27, and the Regulation respecting the application of the Business Corporations Act.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registraire des entreprises du Québec (Québec Enterprise Registrar) — Direction de l'immatriculation et de la publicité légale des entreprises; all filings made through the one-stop Entreprise Québec portal (entreprisequebec.gouv.qc.ca) via clicSéqur.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Statuts de constitution (Articles of Incorporation) filed under the QBCA; the Registry issues the Certificat de constitution (Certificate of Incorporation) and an enterprise register extract (Attestation d'immatriculation) with the Québec Enterprise Number (NEQ).
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital under the QBCA; the authorized capital is defined by the share structure in the articles. Issued shares must be fully subscribed for valid consideration (money, property or services actually rendered) as resolved by the board; no government escrow account or capital-deposit requirement applies, but full payment evidenced by subscription letters is recommended for banking onboarding.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED BY THE FIRST BOARD OF DIRECTORS dated [DATE] (acting by written resolution under s. 118 of the Quebec Business Corporations Act): 1. That the Articles of Incorporation and Certificate of Incorporation issued by the Registraire des entreprises du Québec are recognized, and the registered office is fixed at [civic address], Québec. 2. That ordinary by-law No. 1 is adopted and the officers are appointed: Chief Executive Officer and Secretary-Treasurer. 3. That the subscription agreements for Class A and Class B shares are approved and share certificates issued pro rata to the subscribers; the fiscal year-end is fixed at [date]. 4. That the corporate banking institution is designated and the specimen signature book approved.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) - 'My Business Account' portal (federal administration under the Income Tax Act and the Excise Tax Act for GST/HST) and Revenu Québec (RQ) - 'Mon dossier d'entreprise' portal (administration of the Taxation Act, the Act respecting the Québec sales tax (QST/TVQ), and the collection of federal GST for Quebec-established businesses under the harmonized Canada-Quebec revenue collection agreement).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: 1. File Articles of Incorporation with Corporations Canada (federal) or the Registraire des entreprises du Québec (provincial); the system automatically issues the 9-digit Business Number (BN), which is the primary CRA tax identifier. 2. Register the Quebec establishment with the Registraire des entreprises du Québec to obtain the 10-digit NEQ (Numéro d'entreprise du Québec). 3. Apply through Revenu Québec's converged business registration for the federal RT (GST/HST) program account and the Quebec TVQ (QST) program account; a separate CRA TIN is not required because the operating exporter is a Canadian-resident corporation. 4. Elect voluntary GST/QST registration effective from the date of first expenditure to recover input tax credits during the pre-revenue setup phase. 5. Confirm no CRA non-resident account is needed; the Canadian corporation files T2 (federal) and CO-17 (Quebec) returns using its BN/NEQ. 6. If the company later opens an offshore branch or permanent establishment, file the applicable Form T2201 and Quebec allocation schedules to apportion income.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation - the Quebec business corporation is a Canadian-resident taxpayer subject to full worldwide taxation under ITA Part I (T2) and the Quebec Taxation Act Part I (CO-17). It is not a pass-through entity. Because ultimate shareholders are non-residents, the corporation is a non-Canadian-controlled private corporation (non-CCPC) and cannot access the Small Business Deduction. Dividends paid to foreign shareholders are subject to Part XIII non-resident withholding tax (statutory 25%, generally treaty-reduced to 5-15%). The shares are not taxable Canadian property because the business is an operating service exporter, so no section 116 clearance is required on a future share disposition.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada does not provide a US-style check-the-box election. Relevant statutory elections for this exporter include: (i) ETA s. 156 election for non-calendar GST/QST filing periods; (ii) ETA s. 22/23 closely related corporation election to deem intra-group supplies made for no consideration, simplifying cross-charges; (iii) ETA s. 25 joint venture election if an unincorporated offshore project is structured; (iv) ETA s. 179 reverse-charge election, generally inapplicable to a zero-rated exporter but relevant if the corporation ever imports Canadian-taxable services; (v) foreign affiliate elections under ITA ss. 93(1), 113(1) and Regulation 5902 if an offshore delivery subsidiary is inserted; (vi) hybrid mismatch measures under ITA ss. 18.4 and 18.6 - the corporation may file the s. 18.4(1) election for a qualifying foreign branch to align taxation of certain branch income; (vii) the default combined GST/QST return election with Revenu Québec.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Dual VAT - federal Goods and Services Tax (GST) at 5% and Quebec Sales Tax (QST/TVQ) at 9.975%; Quebec is a non-participating province so no HST component applies; Revenu Québec administers both taxes through a single combined GST/QST return.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 in taxable supplies (including zero-rated export revenues) in a single calendar quarter or over the trailing four consecutive calendar quarters triggers mandatory registration for GST and QST under ETA s. 148 and QST Act s. 210; voluntary registration is advisable before reaching this threshold to recover input tax credits on startup costs.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No mandatory real-time fiscal clearance, no digital stamping, and no tax-authority API approval for invoices in Canada or Quebec. CRA and Revenu Québec accept electronic invoices (XML, PDF, EDI, and increasingly PEPPOL) provided they contain the prescribed disclosure data. Revenu Québec requires electronic filing of GST/QST returns and specified information slips, but not per-invoice pre-clearance. All invoices, credit notes, and export evidence must be retained for six years; each invoice must state: '0% GST/QST - exported service zero-rated under ETA Schedule VI Part V s. 7 / QST Act s. 52.0.1'.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: The supply of custom BIM/CAD engineering drafting services to a non-resident client qualifies for 0% GST/QST under ETA Schedule VI, Part V, section 7 and the equivalent QST Act provision where: (i) the recipient is a non-resident at the time of supply; (ii) the recipient is not registered for GST/HST/QST; (iii) the service is supplied for use exclusively outside Canada and is not performed in respect of real property or tangible personal property situated in Canada; and (iv) the BIM deliverables are transmitted electronically offshore. The contract must characterize the delivery as custom engineering services rather than a licence of standard software, because a pure software licence would remain taxable. Contemporaneous non-resident status evidence must be obtained and retained; absent such evidence, the supply is recharacterized as taxable at the full 14.975% rate and the supplier becomes liable for uncollected tax.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Executed export service agreement expressly identifying the non-resident client, the BIM deliverable scope, the offshore transmission method (portal, FTP, email), and a governing clause confirming performance outside Canada and no connection to Canadian real or movable property
Commercial invoice or XML/PDF e-invoice stating '0% GST/QST - export zero-rated supply under ETA Schedule VI Part V s. 7 / QST Act s. 52.0.1'

Non-resident status evidence: foreign trade register extract, foreign VAT/GST/TIN certificate, or a statutory declaration from the client confirming non-residency and absence of Canadian GST/HST registration
Digital delivery proof: file transfer logs, project-server access logs, IP origin logs, delivery tickets, or signed project handover certificates showing offshore receipt and use
Inward remittance evidence: SWIFT MT103, bank credit advice, or Wise business statement demonstrating receipt of foreign currency settlement from the non-resident client
Customs Export Declaration (B13A) - required only for incidental physical media or hardware prototypes exported; not required for pure digital CAD/BIM service exports
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA and Revenu Québec may reassess within the standard four-year window (extended to ten years for misrepresentation attributable to neglect, carelessness, or wilful default, and unlimited for fraud). If zero-rating is denied, the exporter is assessed for uncollected GST/QST at the combined 14.975% rate plus compounded daily interest, and any input tax credits or refunds previously paid are clawed back. Specific penalties include: (i) failure to register or collect - ETA s. 280, up to CAD 10,000 plus 6% annual interest; (ii) false statements or gross negligence - ETA s. 285, penalty from 50% to 100% of the understated tax, fines up to CAD 50,000 and/or up to two years imprisonment on summary conviction; (iii) parallel penalties under ITA ss. 162/163 and the Quebec Taxation Act, with referral to the CRA Criminal Investigations Program and s. 380 Criminal Code fraud charges carrying up to 14 years imprisonment for deliberately fraudulent export invoicing; (iv) transfer-pricing reassessment under ITA s. 247(3) if export prices deviate from the arm's length range, with associated penalties. The exporter must produce the complete documentation bundle within 30 days of a written audit demand; failure to produce contemporaneous non-resident evidence is treated as an admission that the supply was taxable in Canada.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada), Ottawa, Ontario, is the central monetary authority and exclusive issuer of the Canadian dollar. Canada does not operate a foreign-exchange administration commission or a SAFE-style exchange-control office. Prudential regulation of authorized banks and foreign bank branches is performed by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI). Cross-border fund movement reporting is administered by the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA) and its Regulations. Foreign investment entry controls are administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) under the Investment Canada Act (ICA). Sanctions licensing and enforcement are co-administered by Global Affairs Canada, FINTRAC, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police under the Special Economic Measures Act, the United Nations Act, and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act. Domestic clearing and settlement infrastructure is operated by Payments Canada (Real-Time Rail and the former Large Value Transfer System).
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: CAD is a fully convertible, freely floating fiat currency. Canada has accepted IMF Article VIII obligations, confirming the absence of restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions, and the capital account is de jure open. Inbound equity subscription, shareholder loans, and outbound dividend, interest, royalty, and service payments require no central-bank license, no advance registration, and no currency rationing. Residual obligations are reporting, not permission: (i) FINTRAC international electronic funds transfer (IEFT) reports for every cross-border wire transfer of CAD 10,000 or more; (ii) Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) declaration of physically carried currency or monetary instruments of CAD 10,000 or more; (iii) ICA notification/review for non-Canadian capital injections establishing or acquiring a Canadian business; and (iv) screening against Canadian consolidated sanctions lists. Profit remittance is unimpeded, subject only to Part XIII withholding tax (statutory 25%, treaty-reduced; e.g., 10% or 15% dividends, 10% interest, and 10% royalties under the Canada-China tax agreement) and to transfer-pricing documentation for related-party service and licence fees.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada abolished exchange controls in 1951 and imposes no statutory timeline, no surrender ratio, and no mandatory conversion on export receipts. CA_CORP may invoice its USD or CAD clients in any freely negotiated currency, retain the proceeds in the export account, convert at interbank market rate through any Canadian bank or FINTRAC-registered MSB, and repatriate the balance to non-resident shareholders subject only to corporate-law solvency rules and Part XIII withholding. The sole compliance obligations are: (i) the bank's automatic FINTRAC IEFT report for every cross-border transfer above CAD 10,000; (ii) GST/HST zero-rating records for exported engineering/BIM services supplied to non-residents (Schedule VI, section 9 of the Excise Tax Act), requiring retention of the export contract, invoice, and proof of payment; and (iii) Canadian balance-of-payments classification of the proceeds as computer and information services for Statistics Canada survey purposes.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: High as a supplementary disbursement rail; Low as a replacement for the primary deposit relationship. Wise Inc. (Wise, formerly TransferWise) is registered with FINTRAC as a Money Services Business (MSB) and offers Wise Business multi-currency accounts with CAD, USD, EUR, GBP, and CNY balances, local-currency clearing (Payments Canada EFT, US ACH, SEPA, Faster Payments), and mid-market FX conversion. A Quebec-registered corporation may lawfully use Wise to collect small foreign invoices and to pay foreign subcontractors, subject to four treasury constraints: (i) funds held at Wise are custodial/prepaid obligations, not insured deposits under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, so the monthly float must be capped at the lower of CAD 25,000 or 10% of operating liquidity with a daily sweep back to the Schedule I bank; (ii) every cross-border transfer above CAD 10,000 will be reported by Wise to FINTRAC as an IEFT, creating a parallel data trail that must reconcile with the bank ledger; (iii) Wise cannot execute cheques, letters of credit, payroll tax remittances to CRA or Revenu Quebec, or Part XIII withholding processes, so statutory payments must remain on the bank rail; and (iv) Airwallex, Nium, and Payoneer are also FINTRAC-registered MSBs and viable for niche corridors, but Wise is the only EMI with mature Canadian routing, transparent pricing, and tested compatibility with the target payment rails specified as Wire_Transfer and Wise.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: No federal statute mandates physical presence for corporate account opening. FINTRAC permits remote onboarding where enhanced client due diligence is satisfied through video identity verification, credential-based verification, and notarized/certified documentation. In commercial practice for a foreign-owned Quebec corporation with non-resident directors and a low-risk professional-services profile, the six largest Canadian banks generally require: (i) a registered office and local process agent in Quebec via the Registraire des entreprises du Quebec (REQ); (ii) an in-branch or video interview with the authorized signatory, with final wet-ink signature profiles; (iii) notarization of incorporation documents and beneficial-owner passports by a Quebec notary or lawyer; and (iv) the corporate authorization package (board resolutions, incumbency certificate, share register, UBO registry extract where applicable). RBC and National Bank allow near-digital onboarding with a video callback; TD, BMO, and CIBC prefer an in-person visit to a Montreal-area business banking centre; Desjardins additionally requires the corporation to acquire a permanent membership share. The recommended execution plan is a single two-day Montreal mission visiting National Bank or RBC, completing notarization, and activating the USD and CAD accounts before the first capital injection. Physical presence is thus practically unavoidable for the initial risk rating, but it is not a legal mandate where enhanced remote KYC is accepted by the bank.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) is a non-resident entity or individual; the account is intended primarily for cross-border service receivables, which may trigger shell-company suspicion under FINTRAC CDD guidelines.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Complete corporate closing package: Certificate of Incorporation under the Canada Business Corporations Act or the Quebec Business Corporations Act; Articles of Incorporation with authorized share structure; REQ attestation and current extract; CRA Business Number confirmation letters (GST/HST, payroll, corporate income tax); UBO register extract under the Act respecting the transparency of enterprises (where applicable); certified source-of-wealth statements for every shareholder holding 10% or more; organizational chart tracing control to the ultimate foreign parent; three-year business plan evidencing active BIM and structural drafting delivery; and a financial model projecting monthly transaction volumes and account activity.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-frequency international wire transfers from one or few foreign clients in rapidly repeated tranches, which may appear as layering or structuring under transaction-monitoring analytics.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Framework master service agreement with each principal client; per-project BIM scope-of-work documents; milestone deliverables and transmittal records; an export-invoice ledger mapping every invoice to the corresponding payment confirmation; ISIC 7110 / NAICS 541330 classification statement; evidence that the services are performed in Canada and zero-rated as exported services; and a signed FINTRAC 'trade in services' questionnaire confirming the commercial substance of each inbound transfer.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Use of an EMI (Wise) with rapid in-and-out transfers, or outbound payments to related-party suppliers in jurisdictions subject to enhanced due diligence or sanctions complexity.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Board-approved Treasury Policy restricting Wise to a capped supplementary rail with monthly outflow limits and daily sweeps; a transaction-level sub-ledger of every EMI transfer cross-referenced to invoices; the FINTRAC MSB registration confirmation for Wise; consolidated sanctions screening results for all counterparties verified against Global Affairs Canada lists and, where applicable, OFAC; and board resolutions authorizing all recurring vendor disbursements.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Declaration (Déclaration annuelle) under the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises, including confirmation of the Register of Individuals with Significant Control
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 calendar days after the anniversary of incorporation or amalgamation; reminder month is the incorporation month
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing administrative penalty of CAD 200; if no annual declaration is filed for two consecutive years, the registrar may strike off and dissolve the enterprise; directors may face continued-liability exposure

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Federal Annual Return under section 199 of the Canada Business Corporations Act (required only if the entity is federally incorporated under the CBCA)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporations Canada (Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after each anniversary of incorporation for CBCA corporations
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing fee may apply; failure to file the annual return for two consecutive years allows administrative dissolution by the Director of Corporations Canada after notice

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No statutory revenue or asset threshold triggers an audit for private corporations. A reporting issuer or distributing corporation must appoint a licensed auditor. In a non-distributing private corporation, an audit may be waived each year by a unanimous shareholder resolution.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE) Part II of the CPA Canada Handbook for private businesses; International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) for public or reporting enterprises or by voluntary election.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: The annual declaration to the Registraire des entreprises du Québec must confirm whether the Register of Individuals with Significant Control has been prepared and updated. The register must identify any individual with 25% or more significant control, must be updated within 15 days of a change, and must be available for inspection by relevant authorities without being publicly filed.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Minute Book (resolutions and minutes of directors and shareholders)
Register of Individuals with Significant Control
Securities Register for share transfer records

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 100 – 400 per year for registered office and corporate agent services in Quebec
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 2,500 – 8,000 for a typical engineering services small corporate statutory audit, if audit is not waived

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 26.5% combined general corporate rate for fiscal years ending in 2024 (15% federal Part I general rate + 11.5% Quebec general corporate rate under the Taxation Act (Quebec)). A qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) with active business income benefits from a reduced combined rate.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Federal Small Business Deduction reduces the federal rate to 9% on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income of a CCPC; Quebec applies a reduced SME rate between 3.2% and 5.0% on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income, yielding a combined effective rate of approximately 12.2% to 13.5% for a qualifying Quebec-based CCPC engaged in BIM/CAD drafting. No statutory tax holiday applies to engineering services, but the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program provides refundable/non-refundable investment tax credits (15%-20.75% federal, comparable provincial credits), and Quebec offers the EBI (E-Business) support and the new digital transformation tax credit for recognized technology investments.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (Income Tax Act, Canada) filed electronically via CRA-approved NETFILE software, EDI, or the CRA My Business Account portal (canada.ca/en/revenue-agency). E-filing is mandatory for substantially all active corporations unless an electronic filing waiver is granted.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual fiscal-period return; quarterly/pre-set instalments required where Part I federal tax payable exceeds CAD 3,000; large corporations (taxable capital over CAD 15,000,000) are subject to monthly instalments
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Filing and balance-due date is six months after the fiscal period end (e.g., December 31 year-end is due June 30 of the following calendar year); instalments are due on the last day of each calendar month or on the prescribed quarterly dates; no extension unless the CRA formally waives the time requirement

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Page 1 / Part 1 – Identification and Financial Summary
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Enter the Business Number (BN), program account RC0001, legal name, operating jurisdiction, MNE membership identification, gross revenue, net income, taxable income, and taxes payable
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations must enter the Canadian BN and complete Schedule 21 to claim treaty benefits; include only Canadian-source business income as calculated under section 115 of the Income Tax Act

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Page 4 / Line 560+ (Part 1 – Taxable Income and Federal Tax)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reconcile accounting income to taxable income after adjustments under provisions including sections 110-111, 112, and 113; deduct applicable non-capital losses and capital losses carried forward/back
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Deduct expenses reasonably allocated to the Canadian business through a permanent establishment (PE) as defined in the relevant tax treaty; losses are only deductible against the same source of Canadian income

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Page 4 / Schedule 1 – Federal Tax Calculation and Small Business Deduction
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Apply the 9% small business rate to the qualifying active business income of a CCPC up to the CAD 500,000 annual business limit, and the 15% general rate to the excess; compute the federal abatement and general rate reduction
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations do not qualify for the Small Business Deduction; the 15% general rate applies, and apportionment is based on the provincial PE allocation factor

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Report non-capital losses utilized in the year and amounts available for carryback (3 years) and carryforward (20 years)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident corporation may only deduct losses against Canadian-source income from the same or a substantially similar business

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Claim reduced or exempt treatment under an income tax treaty; attach the NR301/NR601 declarations and the foreign Certificate of Residence supporting the claim
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Mandatory for a non-resident claiming a treaty rate on Canadian-source business income or claiming no PE in Canada; must be supported by the home-country tax authority's Certificate of Residence (TRC)

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 17 and Form T106 – Related-Party Transactions
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Disclose all non-arm's length cross-border transactions involving services, intangibles, financing, and property with a related person where the aggregate exceeds CAD 1,000,000 in the taxation year
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A foreign parent or sister entity engaging in BIM/CAD service streams from the Quebec entity must file T106 and hold contemporaneous transfer-pricing documentation in accordance with CRA's TP policy and fairness procedures

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 9 and Form T1134 – Ownership and CbC Reporting
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Provide control and ownership structure detail for foreign affiliates; country-by-country reporting notification (T1138) and CbC return required for MNE groups with consolidated annual revenue exceeding approximately CAD 1,000,000,000
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Canadian parent of a foreign-held engineering group must disclose foreign affiliates and allocate MNE-source information as prescribed under section 233.7 and related regulations

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late-filing penalty: 5% of the unpaid tax balance plus 1% per full month of delay up to 12 months (10% plus 2% per month for a second or subsequent failure). Gross negligence penalty: 50% of the amount of understated tax. False statements on a T2: 25% to 200% penalties in aggravated cases. Unpaid tax attracts prescribed interest compounded daily. Criminal conviction for failure to file or wilful evasion carries a fine up to CAD 200,000 and imprisonment up to 2 years.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: CO-17 – Corporation Income Tax Return (Revenu Quebec, Act respecting the taxation of municipalities and various legislative provisions) filed through Revenu Quebec's e-filing service 'clicSÉEQ Affaires' at revenuquebec.ca; mandatory e-filing applies to professional corporations and corporate taxpayers with an establishment in Quebec
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual fiscal-period return; instalments required where the corporation's estimated Quebec tax payable exceeds CAD 2,000 (quarterly or monthly for large corporations)
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: CO-17 is due within six months after the end of the fiscal year; any balance due must be paid by that statutory deadline, subject to the instalment scheme

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Enter the total gross revenue reported for Quebec purposes, reconciled to the T2 and financial statements
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident with a permanent establishment in Quebec files CO-17 and allocates revenue to Quebec using the two-factor formula (payroll and gross revenue) prescribed by the Taxation Act (Quebec)

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Start from federal taxable income and adjust for Quebec-specific re-additions and deductions (including provincial loss convergence rules)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Attach the T2 federal return and the Quebec allocation schedules; treaty PE rules govern whether any Canadian PE exists in Quebec

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Line 310 – Taxes Payable / Line 311 – Small Business Rate
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Apply the Quebec general corporate rate of 11.5%; apply the reduced SME rate (3.2%-5.0%) to the qualifying active business income of a CCPC up to CAD 500,000
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The SME rate is inapplicable to non-residents; the full 11.5% applies to income attributable to a Quebec establishment

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Report Quebec non-capital losses carried forward (20 years) or back (3 years) and any capital loss carryforward (5 years)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Quebec losses are only usable against Quebec-source income of the taxpayer, and any claim must respect the federal conformity framework

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Revenu Quebec late-filing penalty is 5% of the unpaid balance plus 1% per full month of delay up to 12 months (sections 1066-1067 of the Taxation Act). Gross negligence penalty of 50% of the understated tax applies to false statements. Unpaid tax bears daily compounded interest at the prescribed provincial rate. Criminal prosecution under section 1054 of the Taxation Act can lead to fines up to CAD 100,000 and imprisonment up to 2 years.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% Part XIII gross tax imposed on dividends paid by a Canadian-resident corporation to any non-resident shareholder (Income Tax Act s. 212(2)). The rate is treaty-reduced: 5% for a US beneficial owner that is a company holding at least 10% of the voting stock and 15% for other US portfolio shareholders (Canada-US DTA Article X); 10% for substantial Canadian-China corporate shareholding and 15% for portfolio dividends (Canada-China DTA Article X).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke DTA relief, the non-resident must (1) obtain an official Certificate of Residence (TRC) from the tax administration of its residence jurisdiction (IRS Form 6166 for the USA; State Taxation Administration Business Residency Certificate for China); (2) complete CRA Form NR301 – Declaration of Eligibility for Benefits under a Tax Treaty (and Quebec Form TP-1000.R-V.0 or NR601 for provincial relief); (3) submit the TRC and signed declaration to the Canadian payer before the dividend remittance so that the payer may apply the reduced withholding rate at source. Where the payer withheld 25% and the treaty rate should have applied, the non-resident must file CRA Form NR7 (Application for Refund of Non-Resident Tax Withheld) within two years of the end of the relevant calendar year, accompanied by the TRC and withholding certificates (CRA form NR4 for Part XIII).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Interest: the 25% statutory Part XIII rate is fully exempt for interest paid to an arm's-length non-resident and to non-residents where the interest is not participating debt (ITA s. 212(1)(b) and (3)); non-arm's length interest remains subject to Part XIII and is reduced by treaty to 0% (Canada-US DTA Article XI) or 10% (Canada-China DTA Article XI). Royalties: 25% statutory Part XIII rate applies to payments for the use of or right to use any copyright, computer software, patent, or technical information; treaty rate is 10% under the Canada-US DTA Article XII for royalties, and 10% under the Canada-China DTA Article XII. BIM/CAD software licensing royalties are treated as copyright royalties where the payment is for the right to reproduce or commercially distribute the software; payments for software used solely for the payer's own internal operations are generally treated as business income.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 1,000,000 aggregate annual value of all non-arm's length cross-border transactions with a related non-resident entity triggers the mandatory filing of Form T106 (Related-Party Transactions). Canada adopts the OECD-aligned Local File and Master File documentation principles; contemporaneous documentation must be prepared and produced to the CRA within three months of a written request. Country-by-Country (CbC) reporting applies to MNE groups with annual consolidated revenue of at least approximately CAD 1,000,000,000 (the CAD equivalent of EUR 750 million), governed by ITA sections 233.7 to 233.74 and the Canada Revenue Agency CbC filing portal.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not administer a standalone Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) regime comparable to the UAE or Bermuda; instead, the general anti-avoidance rule (ITA s. 245) denies tax benefits from avoidance transactions lacking a bona fide business purpose. Corporate residence is a common-law factual determination based on the location of the corporation's central management and control, per the De Beers / Stikeman principles, and the CRA may deem a Quebec-registered shell to be managed from abroad solely to access a treaty or to avoid domestic tax. Anti-treaty-shopping protections appear in Article XXIX-A of the Canada-US DTA (Limitation on Benefits), and the GAAR applies to all artificial structures, including those used by BIM/CAD engineering service providers where the principal purpose is to strip profits through non-arm's length fees paid to offshore or related entities.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion and False Statements (Offshore Billing Scheme)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Wilfully evading Canadian and Quebec income tax by failing to record revenue from foreign BIM/CAD clients, invoicing through non-resident shell entities, diverting payments received via Wire Transfer or Wise to personal accounts outside Canada, or fabricating deductible expenses for services never rendered
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Civil: 50% gross negligence penalty on the understated tax (ITA s. 163(2); Taxation Act (Quebec) s. 1052); 25%-50% penalties for false statements (ITA s. 163(3)); reassessments reopened beyond the normal reassessment period upon misrepresentation; interest compounded daily. Criminal: conviction under ITA s. 239(1)(d) for wilful evasion carries a fine of up to 200% of the tax evaded and imprisonment of up to two years; where the Revenue fraud exceeds CAD 1,000,000, prosecution under Criminal Code s. 380 can result in imprisonment of up to fourteen years.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Quebec Civil Code art. 317 allows the corporate veil to be pierced where the corporation is used for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose; directors or de facto officers who knowingly signed false returns face immediate personal civil liability for the unremitted tax, penalties, and interest; the CRA and Revenu Quebec may issue personal assessments against directors under ITA s. 227.1 and Taxation Act (Quebec) s. 34; in egregious evasion, directors incur criminal exposure and can be prohibited from departing Canada under ITA s. 226.1 when the tax debt exceeds CAD 50,000.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Sham / Shell Company and Treaty Abuse
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Incorporating a Quebec letterbox entity with no office, no employees, no substantive management, and no commercial risk that purports to license BIM/CAD software or services to foreign affiliates for the artificial purpose of avoiding a PE, stripping profits into treaty-favored jurisdictions, or obtaining Quebec investment tax credits through non-qualifying activities
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: GAAR denial of the tax benefit with reassessment of the full amount and interest (ITA s. 245); a penalty of 25% of the avoided tax under s. 245(4)(a), rising to 50% where the arrangement includes a misrepresentation designed to mislead; denial of treaty benefits under Article XXIX-A of the Canada-US DTA; nullification of Quebec deductions; publication of audit findings in CRA's voluntary disclosures context does not apply to fraudulent schemes; civil fraud damages may be asserted by the tax authority.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly permitted the corporation to function as a shell face personal liability for taxes recovered under the veil-piercing doctrine (Civil Code art. 317, 'fraude a la loi'); the CRA may assess directors for the corporation's Part XIII and source deduction liabilities under ITA s. 227.1; travel bans under s. 226.1 apply where a personal assessment remains unpaid; in the case of intentional misrepresentation to extend the reassessment window, directors may be personally criminally liable for conspiracy to defraud the revenue.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Non-Disclosure and Documentation Failure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Billing a US or Chinese parent/affiliated engineering firm for BIM/CAD drafting services at a margin below arm's length without applying an appropriate CUP or TNMM benchmark; failing to file Form T106 for related-party transactions exceeding CAD 1,000,000; refusing to provide the CRA with contemporaneous Local File documentation within three months of the CRA's demand; or entering into circular financing to support fictitious intercompany interest deductions
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Reassessment of taxable income at arm's-length prices plus daily compounded interest; transfer-pricing penalty of 10% of the net adjustment amount where reasonably adequate documentation has not been prepared contemporaneously and retained (ITA s. 247(3)); penalty of CAD 1,000 per month, up to a maximum of CAD 24,000, for failure to respond to a CRA information demand (ITA s. 247(4)); additional 50% gross-negligence penalty where the TP adjustment arises from intentional mispricing; T106 late-filing penalty of CAD 100 for each day of non-compliance up to 25 days, with daily increases after that.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who sign a T2 or CO-17 or any schedule containing false or misleading transfer-pricing information expose themselves to criminal liability under ITA s. 239 and Taxation Act (Quebec) s. 1054; the CRA can separately pursue directors under ITA s. 227.1 for any portion of the corporation's unpaid Part XIII withholdings linked to the arrangement; directors may be named personally in Quebec courts on a 'faute' theory, giving rise to civil restitution orders and exclusion from serving as officers of any Quebec corporation.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Non-Filing, Unremitted Withholdings, and Part XIII Violation
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failure to file the T2 or CO-17 by the statutory six-month deadline; paying dividends to a non-resident shareholder without withholding the 25% Part XIII tax; failing to remit employee source deductions (federal/Quebec income tax, QPP, QPIP, and EI) for locally engaged drafting staff; or redeeming shares in favor of a non-resident shareholder without ancillary withholding
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Late-filing penalties (5% plus 1% monthly surcharge up to 12 months on federal unpaid balance; same structure under Quebec); 10% penalty for failure to remit source deductions, and 20% for repeated unreasonableness (ITA s. 227(8) and (9); Quebec L.T.A. ss. 1067-1071); interest compounded daily; Part XIII failure to withhold renders the payer (Quebec entity) liable for the full 25% of the dividend gross amount as a debt due to the Crown; criminal prosecution of the corporation under ITA s. 239; in aggravated cases, deregistration under the Canada Business Corporations Act and Quebec Business Corporations Act for failure to comply with tax statutes.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are jointly and severally liable for the corporation's unremitted source deductions and Part XIII withholdings under ITA s. 227.1 and Taxation Act (Quebec) s. 34, provided they knew or ought to have known of the failure and did not exercise the 'diligence standard' (due diligence defense); a director who participated in a dividend declaration while knowing the corporation was insolvent faces personal recovery of the entire unpaid withholding plus interest; departure prohibitions under ITA s. 226.1 block international travel for directors with outstanding personal assessments exceeding CAD 50,000; intentional failure can lead to imprisonment for up to two years.
